title: What training became mandatory for nursing care providers in Japan in April 2024?
description: Japan's April 2024 long-term care mandates: abuse prevention training, BCP training and drills, infection prevention training, frequencies and fee reductions.
shortAnswer: From April 1, 2024, every long-term care insurance provider in Japan must run abuse prevention training, training and drills on its business continuity plan, and infection prevention training and drills for staff. These duties were added by MHLW Ordinance No. 9 of 2021 with a three-year grace period. MHLW guidance sets at least one session a year for home and community services and at least two for facilities, and 2024 fee reductions penalize gaps.
keyTakeaways: MHLW Ordinance No. 9 of 2021 amended the operating standards ordinances for long-term care services from April 1, 2021, but treated abuse prevention, business continuity planning (BCP), infection prevention and dementia basic training as effort obligations until March 31, 2024. They became binding on April 1, 2024.

The core articles in the home and community services standards (MHLW Ordinance No. 37 of 1999) are Article 37-2 (abuse prevention), Article 30-2 (BCP) and Article 31(3) (infection prevention); the nursing home standards (Ordinance No. 39 of 1999) mirror them in Articles 35-2, 24-2 and 27(2).

MHLW interpretive notices expect training and drills at least once a year for home and community services and at least twice a year for facilities and specified residential care, with training at hiring and written records.

The fiscal 2024 fee revision added a 1% reduction for providers that have not taken the four abuse prevention measures and a 3% (facilities) or 1% (other services) reduction for providers without a BCP.
Home medical management guidance (kyotaku ryōyō kanri shidō) is the exception: its abuse prevention and BCP duties remain effort obligations until March 31, 2027.
regulator: Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW) Health and Welfare Bureau for the Elderly, with prefectures and municipalities as designating and inspecting authorities
appliesTo: Designated home and community-based long-term care providers, including home-visit care, day care, short stay and specified residential care
Designated long-term care welfare facilities (special nursing homes) and other long-term care insurance facilities
All care workers and other staff, including part-time and registered home helpers
Abuse prevention officers, infection control leads and BCP owners named by each provider

sections.heading: What exactly became mandatory on April 1, 2024?

blocks.text: Four sets of duties moved from "make efforts to" to "must" on April 1, 2024. All four were written into the long-term care operating standards by **MHLW Ordinance No. 9 of 2021** (promulgated January 25, 2021, in force April 1, 2021). Its supplementary provisions rewrote "must take" as "must endeavor to take" until March 31, 2024 for abuse prevention (Article 2), business continuity planning (Article 3), infection prevention for home and community services (Article 4) and dementia basic training (Article 5), giving providers three years to prepare ([home and community services standards, e-Gov](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/411M50000100037)).

blocks.text: One exception remains. The fiscal 2024 amendment (MHLW Ordinance No. 16 of 2024) extended the effort-only treatment of abuse prevention and BCP to March 31, 2027 for home medical management guidance, the visiting physician, dentist, pharmacist and dietitian service. As at November 2026, that service is still in its grace period.

sections.heading: Which laws and ordinances impose the duties?

blocks.text: The duties sit in the MHLW standards ordinances made under the Long-Term Care Insurance Act, which every designated provider must meet to keep its designation. The two most used are the **Standards for Personnel, Equipment and Operation of Designated In-Home Services** (指定居宅サービス等の事業の人員、設備及び運営に関する基準, MHW Ordinance No. 37 of 1999) and the **Standards for Designated Long-Term Care Welfare Facilities** (指定介護老人福祉施設の人員、設備及び運営に関する基準, MHW Ordinance No. 39 of 1999) ([nursing home standards, e-Gov](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/411M50000100039)). Parallel standards cover community-based services, preventive services, care management, geriatric health services facilities and integrated facilities for medical and long-term care.

Underneath sits a statutory duty. Article 20 of the **Act on the Prevention of Elder Abuse and Support for Caregivers** (高齢者虐待防止法, Act No. 124 of 2005) requires founders of care facilities and operators of care businesses to take measures to prevent abuse by their staff, naming staff training and a complaints system. Article 21 requires care staff who discover suspected abuse by a colleague to report it promptly to the municipality and protects them from dismissal for doing so ([Elder Abuse Prevention Act, e-Gov](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/417AC1000000124)). Article 3(3) of the in-home services standards repeats the training duty as a general principle for every provider.

sections.heading: What does abuse prevention training require?

blocks.text: Article 37-2 requires four measures: a committee to consider abuse prevention that meets periodically (video conferencing allowed) and shares its results with staff; a written abuse prevention guideline; periodic abuse prevention training for staff; and a person in charge of implementing these measures. Training is only one of four, but the fee reduction applies if any of the four is missing.

MHLW's interpretive notice for in-home services (老企第25号, as revised in 2021) says training should spread basic knowledge of abuse prevention and apply the provider's own guideline. The provider should build a training program from the guideline, run it periodically at least once a year, and "always" run abuse prevention training at hiring, keeping a record of what was delivered. Internal training is acceptable ([MHLW interpretive notice for in-home services, 2021 revision](https://www.mhlw.go.jp/content/12404000/000772386.pdf)). For special nursing homes, the parallel notice (老企第43号) raises the frequency to at least twice a year, again with mandatory training at hiring ([MHLW interpretive notice for nursing homes, 2021 revision](https://www.mhlw.go.jp/content/12404000/000772408.pdf)). Specified residential care (tokutei shisetsu) is also set at twice a year.

sections.heading: What BCP training and drills are required?

blocks.text: Article 30-2 requires each provider to prepare a business continuity plan for infectious disease outbreaks and natural disasters, follow it, inform staff of it, and run the necessary training and drills periodically, reviewing the plan periodically. Facilities have the same duty under Article 24-2 of the nursing home standards.

The 2021 interpretive notices describe the content. Training should share the specific content of the infection and disaster BCPs, reinforce why preparation matters in normal times and build understanding of the emergency response. Drills (simulations) should confirm role allocation and practice the care to be delivered during an outbreak or disaster. Desk-based and practical drills can be combined. For home and community services the notice sets training and drills at least once a year each, with separate training at hiring described as desirable. For facilities it sets at least twice a year each, with separate training at hiring required. Infection BCP training may be combined with infection prevention training, and disaster BCP drills with fire and disaster evacuation drills.

sections.heading: What infection prevention training is required?

blocks.text: Article 31(3) of the in-home standards requires an infection control committee that meets about once every six months, an infection prevention guideline, and periodic infection prevention training and drills for staff. For special nursing homes, Article 27(2) covers infections and food poisoning and requires the committee to meet about once every three months.

The 2021 interpretive notices again split the frequency. Home and community services should hold infection training at least once a year, with infection training at hiring described as desirable, and run a simulation at least once a year. Facilities should hold training at least twice a year, always run infection training at hiring, and run simulations at least twice a year ([MHLW 2024 comparison table for the nursing home notice](https://www.mhlw.go.jp/content/12300000/001227943.pdf)). MHLW notes that its own infection control training materials for care staff can be used and that in-house delivery is acceptable.

sections.heading: What happens to providers that do not comply?

blocks.text: Since the fiscal 2024 long-term care fee revision, non-compliance costs money every month. MHLW's summary of the revision lists two new reductions to basic fees ([MHLW fiscal 2024 revision items](https://www.mhlw.go.jp/content/12300000/001230329.pdf)):

items: **Reduction for not taking elder abuse prevention measures:** 1% of the prescribed units, applied where any of the four abuse prevention measures (committee, guideline, training, officer) has not been taken. It covers all services except home medical management guidance and specified welfare equipment sales, with a three-year transition for welfare equipment rental.

**Reduction for not implementing a BCP:** 3% for facility and residential services and 1% for other services, applied where an infection or disaster BCP has not been prepared or followed. Until March 31, 2025 it was not applied to providers that had an infection prevention guideline and a disaster plan, and not applied at all to home-visit services, welfare equipment rental and care management.

blocks.text: Beyond fees, the standards are conditions of designation, which prefectures and municipalities check when they guide and audit providers. Training records and committee minutes are the evidence they ask for.

blocks.text: Because the four duties share a committee, guideline, training and drill pattern, many providers combine sessions, which the notices allow in several places. A combined session still needs a record that shows each topic separately. See [how to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles) for scheduling.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry maps each standards article, the matching interpretive notice paragraph and the provider's own guidelines and BCPs as linked obligations, so the training program is derived from the documents an inspector will read. Different frequencies for home services and facilities are held as rules on the obligation, not as separate courses.

faqs.q: Did the April 2024 changes apply to home-visit care as well as nursing homes?
faqs.a: Yes. Abuse prevention, BCP and infection prevention apply to all designated long-term care services, including home-visit care, day care and care management. Only home medical management guidance kept a longer grace period for abuse prevention and BCP, until March 31, 2027. Frequencies differ: at least once a year for home services and twice for facilities.

faqs.q: Can the BCP drill be combined with the fire evacuation drill?
faqs.a: Yes. The 2021 interpretive notices allow drills for the disaster BCP to be combined with drills under the emergency disaster measures, and infection BCP training and drills to be combined with infection prevention training and drills. The record should still show that the BCP content was covered.

faqs.q: Is external training required, or can providers train in-house?
faqs.a: In-house training is acceptable. The interpretive notices state that abuse prevention training may be run within the facility or office, and that infection training may use MHLW's own training materials for care staff. What matters is a training program based on the provider's own guideline and a record of delivery.

faqs.q: Does missing training alone trigger the abuse prevention fee reduction?
faqs.a: It can. The 1% reduction applies where any of the four measures in the standard is not in place: the committee, the guideline, periodic training or the designated officer. A provider with a committee and guideline but no periodic training would not meet the requirement.
